faqs.question: How many marigold flowers do I need for a small Diwali rangoli?
faqs.answer: Plan on about 1.5 kg of loose petals per square metre. A 60 cm doorstep half-moon is about 0.14 square metres, so roughly 250 g of petals, and buy about 20% extra because stripping heads bruises some petals.

faqs.question: Can I make a flower rangoli the night before Diwali?
faqs.answer: Only with marigold and chrysanthemum, and even then expect tired edges by puja time. Rose petals start browning within about 8–12 hours and jasmine loses its scent within 24–36 hours of picking, so add those on the day itself, Friday 29 October 2027.

faqs.question: How do I keep rangoli flowers fresh for longer?
faqs.answer: Keep whole heads cool until you need them and strip petals last. An ICAR review gives ideal storage temperatures of 8–12 °C for marigold and 0–2 °C for rose and chrysanthemum, and warns that ripening fruit gives off ethylene, which speeds wilting.

faqs.question: Which flowers give white in a flower rangoli?
faqs.answer: White sevanti (chrysanthemum), mogra (jasmine) and rajnigandha (tuberose). Sevanti holds longest, about 2–3 days as whole heads; jasmine is an evening-only accent and costs about ₹600–1,500 per kg (EST, Oct 2026).

faqs.question: Is it safe to put diyas on a flower rangoli?
faqs.answer: Put each diya on a steel saucer rather than directly on the petals, and keep jasmine strings and any dried petals clear of the flame. Petals under a diya also soak up oil, so pick those out before composting.

faqs.question: Can I throw rangoli flowers into a river after Diwali?
faqs.answer: Please do not. Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban cites a UN report that the Ganga alone absorbs over 8 million tonnes of flower waste a year; compost the petals, dry them, or hand them to a temple flower-collection programme instead.

faqs.question: Can I dry marigold petals from the rangoli and use them again?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you dry the cleanest ones quickly. A 2023 review reports that dried marigold petals can be made into gulal and that large marigolds dried best at 72 hours in a hot-air oven; shade-drying on newspaper also works but takes longer.

faqs.question: When should I sow marigold seeds to have flowers for Diwali 2027?
faqs.answer: Around 10 August 2027. TNAU says 20-day-old seedlings are transplanted and picking starts 60 days after planting, so transplanting by about 30 August gives flowers by 29 October.

faqs.question: How do I draw a spiral for a petal rangoli?
faqs.answer: Tie chalk to a string, hold the other end at the centre, and let out about 7.5 cm of string for each turn as you walk the chalk round. Five turns fill a 75 cm circle, which needs roughly 700 g of petals.

faqs.question: How can I share my flower rangoli with family in another city?
faqs.answer: Photograph it on Diwali evening while the petals are fresh, since 48.3% of shared SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone. For one person you want to wish properly, the SubhSandesh Diwali card has its own rangoli scene that glows with your initials.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Diwali Rangoli With Flowers: Petal Weights, Freshness, 5 Designs

A Diwali rangoli with flowers needs roughly 1.5 kg of loose petals per square metre for a layer that hides the floor, and it is a same-day job. Marigold petals keep their colour for about a day on a warm floor, rose petals for less, and jasmine starts wilting and losing its scent 24–36 hours after picking. So lay it on the morning of Lakshmi Puja, Friday 29 October 2027, not on Dhanteras.

That last-minute rhythm is familiar from SubhSandesh's own festival data: 49.4% of Raksha Bandhan 2026 pages were built on the festival day itself (n = 89, a different and one-day festival, used here as the nearest analogue). And 48.3% of shared SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone, which is worth knowing if you plan to photograph the rangoli for someone who cannot be there. Below: five flowers compared, five original designs with petal weights, storage temperatures from a 2025 ICAR review, and what to do with the petals on day two.

## What is a flower rangoli, and which flowers suit Diwali?

A flower rangoli is a floor design laid at the threshold or puja corner with loose petals, whole flower heads and leaves instead of coloured powder. It is quicker to fill than powder and smells of the flowers, but it lasts hours rather than days.

Five flowers do almost all the work in Indian markets. A 2025 review in the [Indian Journal of Agricultural Sciences](https://epubs.icar.org.in/index.php/IJAgS/article/view/156841) names marigold, jasmine, chrysanthemum and rose as the loose flowers "integral to religious rituals, festivals, and social ceremonies" in India, and estimates post-harvest losses of 30–40% because they are so perishable. Add tuberose (rajnigandha) for white, plus mango or ashoka leaves for green, and you have a full palette.

Genda (African marigold, *Tagetes erecta*) is the backbone: orange and yellow, cheap, and the slowest to wilt of the five. A genda phool rangoli can be made from marigold alone by using the two colours against each other.

## How long each flower lasts, and why

The review classes rose, jasmine and tuberose as highly sensitive to ethylene, the ripening gas that speeds up wilting, while marigold and chrysanthemum are only moderately sensitive. That one line explains most of what you see on Diwali night: the rose border browns first, the marigold body holds.

Jasmine is the most fragile. [Tamil Nadu Agricultural University's export notes on jasmine](https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/export_import/jasmine/index.html) say the flowers wilt and abruptly lose their fragrance within 24–36 hours of harvest, and that TNAU's improved packing only stretched shelf life from 36 to 72 hours. By the time a string reaches a city flower stall, a good part of that window has gone.

The table compares the five on what matters for a floor design. Hours and prices are planning estimates, not measurements.

| Flower (Hindi name) | Colour in the design | Looks fresh on the floor (EST) | Retail price per kg (EST, Oct 2026) | Ethylene sensitivity (ICAR review) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Marigold (genda) | Orange, yellow | 24–36 hours | ₹80–200 | Moderate |
| Chrysanthemum (sevanti) | White, yellow, maroon | 2–3 days as whole heads | ₹100–250 | Moderate |
| Rose petals (gulab) | Red, pink | 8–12 hours before edges brown | ₹200–400 | High |
| Jasmine (mogra) | White, scent | One evening | ₹600–1,500 | High |
| Tuberose (rajnigandha) | White | About 1 day as florets | ₹200–400 | High |

The takeaway: build the body of the design in marigold and chrysanthemum, and keep rose and jasmine for the last 15 minutes before the puja, where they are seen at their best.

## Five flower rangoli designs, with petal weights

Each design lists size and petals, time, steps, and how long it lasts. Weights assume about 1.5 kg of loose petals per square metre; buy 20% extra, because stripping heads leaves bruised petals you will not use.

### 1. Doorstep half-moon in three bands

**Size and petals:** 60 cm wide, 30 cm deep (0.14 m²); about 250 g, split into yellow genda, orange genda and white sevanti. **Time:** 15–20 minutes. **Steps:** Draw the half-circle with chalk against the door frame, then two inner arcs 10 cm apart. Fill the outer band yellow, the middle orange and the inner white, and set three diyas along the straight edge. **Lasts:** a day; the white band yellows first.

### 2. Four-diya pinwheel square

**Size and petals:** 60 cm square (0.36 m²); about 550 g of orange genda and red rose petals. **Time:** 30–40 minutes. **Steps:** Chalk the square and both diagonals to get four triangles. Fill opposite triangles orange and the other two red, then turn each red triangle into a blade by curving its outer edge with a line of yellow petals. Put a diya on a steel saucer at each corner and one sevanti head at the centre. **Lasts:** the orange holds a day; refresh the red with new petals for night two.

### 3. Petal spiral with a mogra line

**Size and petals:** 75 cm circle (0.44 m²); about 700 g of genda plus one 1-metre mogra string. **Time:** about 45 minutes. **Steps:** Tie chalk to a string and draw a five-turn spiral from the centre, each turn about 7.5 cm apart. Fill alternate turns yellow and orange, then lay the mogra string along the chalk line between them. **Lasts:** a day; the jasmine is an evening-only accent.

### 4. Kalash corner for a flat's landing

**Size and petals:** quarter circle of 50 cm radius (0.2 m²); about 300 g of genda and sevanti plus 15 mango leaves. **Time:** 25 minutes. **Steps:** Outline a pot shape in the corner with orange petals, fill it yellow, and fan the mango leaves from its mouth as the kalash's leaves. A single sevanti head becomes the coconut. **Lasts:** the leaves stay green two days; the petals one.

### 5. Thali rangoli you can carry indoors

**Size and petals:** a 40 cm steel thali (0.13 m²); about 200 g of mixed petals. **Time:** 15 minutes. **Steps:** Make concentric rings from the rim inwards and set one diya in the centre. On a shared building corridor where the floor gets swept or walked on, this is the only version that survives, because you can lift the whole design into a cooler room overnight. **Lasts:** two evenings with a light water mist, a household practice rather than a tested one.

## Buying and storing petals for Diwali 2027

Buy whole heads on the morning of Friday 29 October 2027, or late on Choti Diwali, Thursday 28 October, and strip the petals last. Stored flowers keep best near their ideal temperature, and the ICAR review lists them: marigold 8–12 °C, jasmine 4–7 °C, tuberose 4 °C, and rose and chrysanthemum 0–2 °C. A home fridge is close enough for rose and sevanti overnight; marigold is happier in the coolest room of the house.

Keep the flowers away from the fruit bowl. Ripening fruit gives off ethylene, and the review notes that air containing just 100 ppb of ethylene harms flowers, with rose and jasmine the worst affected.

If you want your own genda, plan backwards. The [TNAU marigold crop guide](https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/horticulture/horti_flower%20crops_marigold.html) says flowers are picked once every 3 days from 60 days after planting, using 20-day-old seedlings. For a 29 October harvest that means transplanting by about 30 August 2027 and sowing seed around 10 August.

## Eco disposal: what to do with the petals on day two

Do not tip the petals into a river, lake or drain. The Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban's [floral waste feature](https://sbmurban.org/petals-to-profit) cites a UN Climate Change report that the Ganga alone absorbs over 8 million tonnes of flower waste a year, and notes that Tirupati's municipal corporation handles over 6 tons of temple flowers every day.

At home, three routes work. Mix petals with dry leaves and soil in a compost pot or a society compost pit, after picking out any thread from jasmine strings and any wax or oil-soaked petals from under the diyas. Or dry the best marigold petals: a [2023 review of flower drying](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC10225293) reports that ICAR encouraged farmers to dry marigolds and roses rather than destroy them, that dried petals can be made into gulal, and that large marigolds dried best at 72 hours in a hot-air oven. Spread on newspaper in the shade, they take several days longer but need no oven.

The third route is to hand them over. Many cities now run temple flower collection under Swachh Bharat, so ask your local temple whether it accepts household petals.

## When a flower rangoli is the wrong choice

A flower rangoli is wrong if you need one design for all five days, from Dhanteras on Wednesday 27 October to Bhai Dooj on Sunday 31 October 2027. Petals will not last that long; rice paste or powder will. It is also a poor fit on an open, windy balcony, and expensive if you lean on jasmine at ₹600–1,500 per kg (EST).

It is also the wrong way to reach someone who is not at home for Diwali, because a rangoli is a thing you stand beside. For that one person, SubhSandesh's [Diwali card where they colour a rangoli until your initials glow](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-diwali) carries the gesture to their phone. It is a greeting page, not a design tool: it will not plan your floor, and it takes about 5 minutes to set up.

If the person you are thinking of is a partner far away and you want flowers rather than a festival scene, the [digital bouquet page](https://subhsandesh.in/bouquet-gf), where you hand-tie a bouquet from 12 blooms and send a link that opens when tapped, is the closer fit. It is SubhSandesh's second most-made page type, with 1,190 created, and it does not wilt by morning.

- Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, Agritech Portal, "Jasmine" export technology (no date published): [agritech.tnau.ac.in](https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/export_import/jasmine/index.html)
- Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, Agritech Portal, "Marigold" crop guide (no date published): [agritech.tnau.ac.in](https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/horticulture/horti_flower%20crops_marigold.html)
